Subject: Connectivity options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Jordan,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. Acme's infra team asked me to get a concise recommendation from Redwood: for our Private deployment (VPC in our AWS account + some on-prem appliances) should we pursue VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink, or a site-to-site VPN?

Quick constraints:
- PCI-scope workloads, so we need strong separation and auditability.
- Latency target for inference calls: <25ms median from our app tier (same region).
- We plan to keep most data in our VPC but have a small on-prem DC that will also call the service.
- We prefer a single pattern (or clear primary + fallback) rather than many ad-hoc links.

Can you outline tradeoffs and a recommended path so I can present to our security & network teams? Also happy to share a network sketch if that helps.

Thanks,
Lena

Hi Lena — great question. High level summary up front: PrivateLink as the primary path + a site-to-site (S2S) VPN as a documented failover gives you the best mix of security, single-tenant control, and predictable latency for your PCI workloads. VPC Peering is simple but has cross-account management and routing limits that make it less attractive for auditable, multi-tenant hosting patterns.

I'm attaching a short playbook (one-page) that sketches the recommended pattern and what we'd need from your side. Key bullets below; I can schedule 30 mins with your networking folks to walk through specifics:

- PrivateLink (primary):
  - Pros: strong isolation (endpoint service), no cross-account route exposure, easier IAM + security group controls, straightforward logging via VPC Flow + service-side tracing.
  - Cons: requires endpoint creation in your VPC; egress costs apply per GB on endpoint; we need mutual TLS at the application layer for end-to-end auth.
- S2S VPN (fallback):
  - Pros: quick to set up for the on-prem DC and provides resilient path if the endpoint has issues; good for burst or management access.
  - Cons: not as predictable latency under heavy load, MTU & jumbo-frame considerations, and we recommend BGP for dynamic failover which will add config complexity.
- VPC Peering:
  - Best for cases where both accounts will share lots of internal subnets and services. For your PCI needs we worry about expanded blast radius and auditability; peering also complicates cross-account route policies and transitive routing.

Next steps: if you share a CIDR/route table sketch and whether you want the endpoint in a private subnet or a dedicated management subnet, we can produce a short technical design and an SOW for work to configure and test.

I'll loop in Marissa from our deployments team to weigh in on MTU/BGP and expected testing windows.

—Jordan

Subject: FW: Connectivity options for Redwood Private deployment — tradeoffs & ops checklist

Marissa / Ben — forwarding Lena's ask and my quick reply. Below are the operational tradeoffs I want to capture for the technical design and pilot. Please comment / correct.

Summary recommendation (my thinking): PrivateLink primary (endpoints in customer VPC) + S2S VPN as secondary/failover. We offer a managed endpoint service that lives in our account; customer creates an interface endpoint in their VPC.

Operational bullets:
- Security & auditability:
  - PrivateLink keeps the dataplane tethered to the endpoint, reducing cross-account route exposure — aligns with PCI needs.
  - We will require mTLS between the customer and our inference instances; use short-lived certs rotated via the customer's KMS (or Redwood's if agreed).
- Latency & performance:
  - PrivateLink keeps hops minimal inside AWS fabric and typically meets sub-25ms median for same-region app tier; must size endpoint ENIs appropriately for bursty traffic.
  - VPN can introduce variable latency; recommend it only as failover or for low-rate admin traffic.
- Networking operational items:
  - MTU: ensure 1500 vs 9001 checks if customer's on-prem appliances expect jumbo frames — will need fragmentation policy.
  - BGP: if using VPN failover, prefer dynamic BGP peering for route convergence; document ASNs and route filters.
  - IP management: ask for dedicated /28 for endpoint ENIs and explicit route table entries to avoid accidental exposure.
- Cost/charging notes for sales:
  - PrivateLink endpoint egress will be billable — approximate 1–2% uplift on monthly token/GB bill depending on throughput. Need to surface this in SOW.
  - VPN cost is typically lower but operational overhead is higher for consistent low-latency requirements.
- Test plan:
  - Step 1: Create endpoint in staging VPC + smoke tests (latency, TLS handshakes, trace IDs).
  - Step 2: Failover test — bring down endpoint and confirm VPN route convergence within agreed windows.
  - Step 3: Load test to confirm ENI scaling and token throughput.

Marissa: can you draft a short playbook (2 pages) for the customer that includes the exact config snippets (ENI sizing, security group rules, CIDR examples) and a proposed testing timetable? Ben: flag any commercial language we should add for the SOW (eg. egress estimates, roll-out assist hrs).

—Jordan

We are fine with PrivateLink as the primary connectivity; we'll provision the interface endpoints in our PCI VPC in private subnets and keep the S2S VPN for on-prem DR and as an explicit fallback. A couple of asks before we kick off:

- We use DocuSign for all SOWs — please send the link when ready.

If you can get the SOW & playbook over by EOD Monday, our security folks will meet Tuesday and we can schedule the pilot for the following week.

Thanks — looking forward to getting started.
